def: Selling ownership (shares). Shareholders get the upside if the company does well but are paid last if it fails.

Borrowing money. Lenders get a fixed return and are paid before shareholders, but they don't share in the upside. Because lenders have no upside, they protect themselves with contract terms. Those terms are what deal-data platforms benchmark.
Both are debt securities sold to investors. "Notes" traditionally meant shorter maturities, but in practice the terms are used interchangeably. Most high-yield deals are called "Senior Notes."
One company buying or combining with another. Governed by a merger agreement (Section 8).
The question lawyers ask during negotiation: what is typical for comparable deals right now? Answering it requires extracting the same term from many contracts and comparing them.
why: This is the core of what deal-data platforms sell. A typical task is to compute a distribution (median, percentiles) of a term or flag deals that are "off market."

def: The amount borrowed and repaid at the end. Here, $500 million.
why: Indentures also mention the minimum denomination (often $2,000 or $1,000). A parser that grabs that number instead of the deal size is a common bug.

def: 100% of face value. Prices are quoted as a percentage of par, so "redeem at 101%" means paying $1,010 per $1,000 bond.
The annual interest, here 7.50%, usually paid in two semi-annual installments.
When the principal must be repaid, here 2031. High-yield bonds typically mature 5–10 years after issue.
One hundredth of a percent (0.01%). "+350bps" means 3.50 percentage points above a benchmark rate.

The contract governing a bond issue, between the issuer and a trustee. It sets out the payment terms, redemption rights, covenants and events of default. Often 100+ pages, organized into numbered articles and sections (e.g. "Section 4.10 Change of Control").
why: This is the document you'd download and parse to extract bond terms. On EDGAR it is usually filed as Exhibit 4.x.

def: The company that borrows by selling the bonds.
A bank (e.g. U.S. Bank, Wilmington Trust, Computershare) that represents all bondholders. Thousands of investors can't negotiate individually, so the trustee enforces the indenture on their behalf.
Where the debt ranks in the repayment line during bankruptcy. Senior debt is paid before subordinated (junior) debt.

Secured debt is backed by collateral (specific assets lenders can seize), like a mortgage. Unsecured debt has no collateral. "Senior secured" is the safest position; "senior unsecured" is first in line among unsecured lenders.
An agency's grade (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) of how likely a borrower is to repay. S&P's scale runs AAA, AA, A, BBB, BB, B, CCC and down.
Investment grade = rated BBB- or higher: safer, lower coupons, few covenants. High yield ("junk") = below BBB-: riskier, higher coupons, heavy covenants.
why: Most of the interesting "what's market" analysis is in high yield, where covenants are negotiated deal by deal.

def: Exemptions that let companies sell bonds without a full public registration. 144A covers sales to large US institutions ("qualified institutional buyers"); Reg S covers sales outside the US. Most high-yield bonds are sold this way.
why: Because 144A deals aren't registered, the indenture often appears on EDGAR only as an exhibit to an 8-K filed after closing.

def: The issuer's right to repay ("call") the bonds before maturity at a set price.
An initial window, often 2–3 years for high yield (described as "NC2" or "NC3"), when the bonds can't be called at normal prices.
After the non-call period, the call price starts above par and falls each year to par.
ex: Callable at 103.750% in year 3, 101.875% in year 4, and 100% thereafter. The first call premium is often half the coupon.

def: During the non-call period, the issuer can still repay, but only by paying the present value of every remaining coupon (discounted at a Treasury rate plus a small spread, e.g. T+50bps). It's so expensive that it's effectively a penalty.
An exception letting the issuer redeem a slice of the bonds early, usually up to 35–40%, using cash from a stock sale, at par plus one year's coupon.
A defined event in which the company gets a new owner, e.g. an acquirer buys more than 50% of the voting stock, or the company sells substantially all its assets.

Bondholders' right to force the company to buy back their bonds if a change of control occurs, almost always at **101%** of principal plus accrued interest. Protects lenders from a new owner who might load the company with more debt.
why: 101% is so standard that any other value is "off market," which makes it a classic field to extract and benchmark.

def: Common in investment-grade bonds: holders can sell back only if there's a change of control **and** a ratings downgrade. Weaker protection than the high-yield single trigger.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. A rough proxy for the cash a business generates from operations. Most covenant tests are built on it.
Total debt ÷ EBITDA. "4.0x levered" means debt equals four years of EBITDA. Higher = riskier.
EBITDA ÷ interest expense. How many times over earnings cover interest payments. Lower = riskier. A typical test: coverage of at least 2.0x.
A test the borrower must pass every quarter, like a quarterly checkup. Failing is a default even if the company did nothing new. Typical of bank loans.
ex: "Leverage must not exceed 4.5x at the end of any fiscal quarter."

def: A test checked only when the borrower tries to do something, such as borrow more or pay a dividend. Like a bouncer at a door: business can worsen and nothing triggers. Typical of bonds.
A size-capped exception to a covenant.
ex: "No additional debt, except up to the greater of $100 million and 15% of EBITDA."

def: A basket sized as the greater of a fixed dollar amount and a percentage of EBITDA or assets, so it grows with the company. The "15% of EBITDA" part above.
Capacity that accumulates over time, usually 50% of cumulative net income since the deal closed, which the company can later use for restricted payments.
Permission to borrow without a dollar cap as long as a ratio test is met after the borrowing.
ex: "The company may incur debt if, after doing so, its fixed charge coverage ratio would be at least 2.0x."

def: Adjustments that increase the EBITDA used in covenant tests, such as expected cost savings from a merger not yet completed. Higher EBITDA means more ratio capacity and bigger grower baskets.
why: Uncapped add-backs are a borrower-friendly term that lawyers benchmark closely.

def: A loan with no maintenance covenants, so it behaves like a bond. Now the norm for large leveraged loans.

Restricted subsidiaries are bound by the covenants and support the debt. Unrestricted subsidiaries sit outside the covenants, so assets moved there are out of lenders' reach. Central to the J.Crew story in Section 7.
The contract governing a loan. On EDGAR usually filed as Exhibit 10.x.
The company taking the loan.
The banks and funds providing the money. A large loan is split among a group, the syndicate.
The bank that runs the loan for the syndicate: collects payments, distributes them and handles notices. Plays roughly the role a trustee plays for bonds.

Other entities, usually the borrower's subsidiaries, that promise to repay if the borrower can't. Guarantees give lenders claims against the subsidiaries' assets. Their release is central to the Chewy story in Section 7.
A credit line the company draws, repays and redraws as needed, like a corporate credit card.
Borrowed all at once and repaid in steady installments. Held mainly by banks.
Borrowed all at once with only small (often 1% per year) repayments until maturity. Sold to institutional investors such as CLO funds. The workhorse of leveraged finance.
A floating interest rate. SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) is the benchmark short-term US rate that replaced LIBOR. The margin (spread) is fixed in the contract.
ex: SOFR of 4.3% + a 3.00% (300bps) margin = 7.3% for that period.

def: A table that lowers the margin as leverage improves.
Maintenance tests in a credit agreement, most commonly a maximum leverage ratio and a minimum interest coverage ratio.
Events that let lenders demand immediate repayment ("acceleration"): missed payments, covenant breaches, bankruptcy and similar.
A default on other debt (above a size threshold) also counts as a default under this agreement, so one default can topple all of a company's debt.

If the company later adds a new loan at a higher rate, existing lenders' rate is bumped up to within a cushion of it, often 50bps. The negotiation is over the size of the cushion and how long the protection lasts (the "sunset").
A transaction where a struggling company uses flexibility in its own debt contracts to raise new money or cut its debt, often at the expense of some existing lenders.
Contract language added to close a specific loophole. Each well-known one is named after the case that exposed the loophole.
J.Crew moved valuable brand IP into an unrestricted subsidiary, outside the covenants, and borrowed against it. A J.Crew blocker bars moving material IP to unrestricted subsidiaries.

Serta's majority lenders cut a side deal that put their debt ahead of the minority's (a non-pro-rata "uptier" exchange). A Serta blocker requires every affected lender's consent before changing repayment priority.

PetSmart transferred shares of its subsidiary Chewy so Chewy was no longer wholly owned, which under the contract automatically released Chewy's guarantee of the debt. A Chewy blocker stops a guarantee being released just because a subsidiary stops being wholly owned.
The contract to acquire a company. On EDGAR usually filed as Exhibit 2.1 to an 8-K.
Statements of fact one side makes about itself ("our financial statements are accurate," "there is no undisclosed litigation"). If they prove false, the other side may be able to walk away.
What must be true before the deal completes: regulatory approval, a shareholder vote, reps still accurate, no MAE.

The buyer's escape hatch if the target's business suffers a severe, lasting hit before closing. The carve-outs are what matter: general economic downturns, pandemics and industry-wide problems usually don't count. Courts very rarely find that an MAE occurred.
What the target pays the buyer if the deal ends for certain reasons, typically because the target accepts a better offer. Usually about 2–4% of deal value.
What the buyer pays the target if the buyer can't close, e.g. because financing or regulatory approval fails.
The deadline after which either side can terminate if the deal hasn't closed. Often extendable for pending regulatory approvals.
Bars the target from soliciting or negotiating with other bidders after signing.
Lets the target actively seek better offers for a set window (often 30–45 days) after signing, usually with a lower termination fee for a bidder found in that window.
The target board's right to accept a superior unsolicited offer despite the no-shop, because directors owe duties to shareholders. Using it usually triggers the termination fee.
The SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system. Every public filing since the mid-1990s is available at sec.gov.
A company's permanent numeric ID. APIs often require it zero-padded to 10 digits.
The unique ID of one filing, formatted filer-ID-year-sequence. It forms part of every document's URL.

Each 8-K says which events it reports by item number. Key ones: **Item 1.01** entry into a material definitive agreement; **Item 2.03** creation of a direct financial obligation (new debt); **Item 9.01** financial statements and exhibits (the list of attachments).

Attachments follow a standard scheme: **2.x** merger and acquisition agreements; **4.x** instruments defining security holders' rights, including indentures; **10.x** material contracts, including credit agreements.
why: Filtering filings by exhibit type is how you'd find indentures without opening every 8-K.

def: Quarterly lists of every filing (company, form type, date, path), under sec.gov/Archives/edgar/full-index/YEAR/QTRn/ (e.g. form.idx, master.idx). The simplest way to enumerate all 8-Ks in a quarter.
A per-company JSON file of its filing history at data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK##########.json. Best when you start from a list of companies.
Keyword search across the text of filings since 2001 (EDGAR full-text search, backed by an efts.sec.gov API). Useful for finding filings containing phrases like "indenture" and "change of control."
Each filing's landing page listing every document in it with its exhibit type. Where you identify which file is Exhibit 4.1.
Nightly zip archives of all submissions JSON and all XBRL company facts. Gigabytes in size, so download them with streaming, resumable logic.

XBRL is the tagged, machine-readable format for financial-statement numbers in filings. "Company facts" (data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/) gives every reported value per company, e.g. revenue by period.

SEC rules for automated access: send a descriptive User-Agent header with your name or company and contact email, and stay at or under 10 requests per second. Violations get 403 errors or temporary blocks.
why: Claude Code often forgets the User-Agent at first. Catching that, and adding rate limiting, is a visible judgment signal.

def: Running a step twice produces the same result as running it once, with no duplicates and no corruption. Achieved with stable IDs (e.g. accession number + exhibit) and upserts instead of blind inserts.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: A long job can stop and restart without redoing finished work, e.g. skipping files already on disk.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: A backfill loads all historical data once. An incremental load processes only what's new since the last run (e.g. the latest quarter).
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Being able to trace every value back to where it came from: source document, URL and section, and which code version extracted it. Any platform that promises "verifiable data" depends on it.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: The shape of incoming data changing over time (renamed columns, new fields, changed types). Pipelines should detect it and fail loudly or adapt, never silently corrupt.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Removing duplicate records, e.g. amended filings or the same indenture re-filed as a 10-K exhibit.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Explicit checks on data, such as no negative amounts, dates in range or required fields present, with counts of how many rows fail each rule.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: A tamper-evident log of who accessed or changed what, and when. Required in regulated environments.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, people can demand deletion of their personal data. Platforms need to find and delete it everywhere it lives, including derived tables, indexes and backups.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Personally identifiable information (names, emails, addresses, ID numbers). Usually must be minimized, masked in logs and access-controlled.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Splitting long documents into smaller pieces for search or LLM processing. For contracts, chunk by section heading rather than by fixed character count, so each chunk is one meaningful provision.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Numeric vectors representing a text's meaning, so similar meanings land close together even when the words differ.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Ranks documents by matching words, weighting rare terms higher. BM25 is the standard scoring formula. Precise for exact phrases, but misses paraphrases.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Ranks by embedding similarity, so it finds paraphrases, but can miss exact terms like a section number.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Combines keyword and semantic scores (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) to get the strengths of both.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: A small hand-labeled set of correct answers used to measure an extraction or search system.
section: 10. Data platform concepts to name out loud

def: Precision: of the values the system returned, how many were correct. Recall: of the values that should have been found, how many were. Report both, per field.
ex: If you extract a CoC price from 40 of 50 indentures and 38 are right: precision = 38/40 = 95%, recall = 38/50 = 76%.
